question: In restricted visibility (fog, heavy rain, haze, etc.), what must every vessel do under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing conditions, and a power-driven vessel must have her engines ready for immediate maneuver
choice_b: Stop immediately and wait for visibility to improve before moving at all
choice_c: Maintain full cruising speed since radar can compensate for reduced visibility
choice_d: Right-of-way rules no longer apply once visibility drops below one mile
explanation: Rule 19 requires every vessel in or near an area of restricted visibility to proceed at a safe speed adapted to the conditions, and a power-driven vessel must keep her engines ready for immediate maneuvering in case quick action is needed to avoid a collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules conduct in restricted visibility (Rule 19(b), 33 CFR 83)

question: If an operator in restricted visibility hears, apparently forward of the beam, the fog signal of another vessel, what must they do?
choice_a: Increase speed to pass the area where the other vessel is located as quickly as possible
choice_b: Reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course, and take all way off if necessary, navigating with extreme caution
choice_c: Ignore the signal unless the other vessel is visible
choice_d: Immediately alter course to port toward the sound
explanation: Rule 19 requires a vessel that hears another vessel's fog signal apparently forward of its beam to reduce speed to the minimum needed to maintain steerage, and to take all way off if necessary, until the risk of collision is over.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules restricted visibility fog-signal response (Rule 19(e), 33 CFR 83)

question: When traveling along a narrow channel or fairway, such as an inlet or dredged channel on the New Jersey coast, where should a vessel keep to as far as safe and practicable?
choice_a: As near to the center of the channel as possible regardless of other traffic
choice_b: As near to the outer limit on her own port (left) side as is safe and practicable
choice_c: As near to the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard (right) side as is safe and practicable
choice_d: Wherever the water is deepest, even if that means crossing to the far side
explanation: Rule 9 requires a vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway to keep as near as is safe and practicable to the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard side, similar to keeping to the right on a roadway.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules narrow channels (Rule 9(a), 33 CFR 83)

question: Under Rule 9, what obligation applies to a vessel less than 20 meters long or a sailing vessel when it comes to a larger vessel that can only navigate safely within a narrow channel or fairway?
choice_a: Small vessels and sailing vessels always have the right-of-way in a narrow channel
choice_b: The larger vessel must always yield to smaller vessels in a narrow channel
choice_c: There is no special rule for narrow channels beyond the ordinary crossing rule
choice_d: The smaller vessel or sailing vessel must not impede the passage of the vessel that can only navigate safely within the channel
explanation: Rule 9 specifically states that a vessel under 20 meters or a sailing vessel must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway, because the larger vessel has little room to maneuver.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules narrow channels (Rule 9(b), 33 CFR 83)

question: May a vessel cross a narrow channel or fairway, such as an ICW section along the New Jersey coast, whenever it wants to?
choice_a: No -- a vessel must not cross a narrow channel or fairway if doing so would impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel
choice_b: Yes, crossing traffic always has the right-of-way over traffic running along the channel
choice_c: Yes, as long as the crossing vessel sounds one short blast first
choice_d: No, crossing a narrow channel is never permitted under any circumstance
explanation: Rule 9 prohibits a vessel from crossing a narrow channel or fairway if that crossing would impede the passage of a vessel that can only navigate safely within the channel, since such vessels have very limited room to maneuver around crossing traffic.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules narrow channels (Rule 9(d), 33 CFR 83)

question: When a vessel is nearing a bend in a narrow channel or fairway where an intervening obstruction may hide other traffic, what must it do?
choice_a: Speed up to clear the bend before another vessel can appear
choice_b: Navigate with particular alertness and caution, and sound one prolonged blast, which any approaching vessel within hearing around the bend must answer with a prolonged blast
choice_c: Sound five short blasts and hold course regardless of other traffic
choice_d: There is no special signal or precaution required at a blind bend
explanation: Rule 9 requires extra caution near a blind bend and requires sounding one prolonged blast, per the whistle signal in Rule 34(e); any vessel that may be approaching around the bend and hears the signal must answer with a prolonged blast of its own.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules narrow channel bend signal (Rule 9(f) and Rule 34(e), 33 CFR 83)

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel making way through the water sound, and how often?
choice_a: Two short blasts at intervals of not more than 30 seconds
choice_c: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_d: No sound signal is required if the vessel has functioning radar
explanation: Rule 35 requires a power-driven vessel making way through the water in restricted visibility to sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, so nearby vessels that cannot see it can be alerted to its presence and movement.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals in restricted visibility (Rule 35(a), 33 CFR 83)

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal does a power-driven vessel that is underway but has stopped and is making no way through the water sound?
choice_a: One prolonged blast, the same signal as a vessel making way
choice_b: One short and one prolonged blast repeated continuously
choice_c: No signal, since a stopped vessel poses no collision risk
choice_d: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with an interval of about 2 seconds between them, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
explanation: Rule 35 distinguishes a power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water, which must sound two prolonged blasts in succession about 2 seconds apart, from a vessel making way, which sounds a single prolonged blast.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals in restricted visibility (Rule 35(b), 33 CFR 83)

question: In restricted visibility, a sailing vessel, a vessel engaged in fishing, a vessel not under command, or a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver must sound what signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes?
choice_a: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
explanation: Rule 35 requires vessels not under command, restricted in ability to maneuver, engaged in fishing, or sailing vessels underway to sound one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes in restricted visibility, distinguishing them from an ordinary power-driven vessel underway.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals in restricted visibility (Rule 35(c), 33 CFR 83)

question: In restricted visibility, how must a vessel at anchor signal her position?
choice_a: By sounding one prolonged blast every 2 minutes, the same as an underway vessel
choice_b: By ringing a bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute
choice_c: By turning on all deck lights and staying silent
choice_d: No signal is required for an anchored vessel in fog
explanation: Rule 35 requires a vessel at anchor in restricted visibility to ring a bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute to warn nearby traffic of her fixed position, since her whistle signal alone would not distinguish her from a vessel underway.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules sound signals in restricted visibility (Rule 35(e), 33 CFR 83)

question: When two power-driven vessels are in sight of one another and one intends to leave the other on her own port side while altering course to starboard, what whistle signal must she sound?
explanation: Rule 34 assigns one short blast to mean 'I intend to leave you on my port side,' while two short blasts mean 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side,' letting nearby vessels in sight of one another announce a course change before making it.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules maneuvering and warning signals (Rule 34(a), 33 CFR 83)

question: If an operator in sight of another vessel is in doubt about whether the other vessel is taking sufficient action to avoid a collision, what must the operator do?
choice_a: Say nothing and wait to see what the other vessel does
choice_b: Sound one prolonged blast only, then take no further action
choice_c: Flash the vessel's running lights on and off repeatedly instead of sounding a signal
choice_d: Immediately signal that doubt by sounding at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle
explanation: Rule 34 requires an operator who is in doubt as to whether another vessel is taking sufficient action to avoid collision to immediately signal that doubt with at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle, a signal commonly called the danger or doubt signal.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules danger/doubt signal (Rule 34(d), 33 CFR 83)

question: Under Rule 7, when should an operator generally consider that risk of collision with an approaching vessel exists?
choice_a: When the compass bearing of the approaching vessel does not appreciably change, even though risk can still exist when a bearing does change, especially when approaching a very large vessel, a tow, or at close range
choice_b: Only when the other vessel is close enough to be seen without binoculars
choice_c: Only after the other vessel sounds a whistle signal
choice_d: Risk of collision cannot be determined until the vessels are within 100 yards of each other
explanation: Rule 7 states that risk of collision generally exists when the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change, but warns that risk can still exist despite an appreciable bearing change, particularly with a very large vessel, a tow, or a vessel at close range, and that assumptions should never be made on scanty information.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules risk of collision (Rule 7, 33 CFR 83)

question: Which of the following is a factor every vessel must consider when determining a safe speed under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Only the posted speed limit for the waterway
choice_b: The state of visibility, traffic density, and the vessel's own stopping distance and turning ability
choice_c: Only the horsepower of the vessel's engine
choice_d: Safe speed is a fixed number of miles per hour that never changes with conditions
explanation: Rule 6 lists factors such as visibility, traffic density, the vessel's maneuverability including stopping distance and turning ability, background lighting at night, and the state of wind, sea, and current, all of which must be weighed together to determine a safe speed for the prevailing circumstances.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules safe speed (Rule 6, 33 CFR 83)

question: Do the Navigation Rules that apply on New Jersey waters change depending on location?
choice_a: No, the same identical rule set applies everywhere on earth's navigable waters with no boundary lines
choice_b: The switch between rule sets is left entirely to each boat operator's personal preference
choice_c: Yes -- federal COLREGS Demarcation Lines drawn across NJ inlets and bays, such as at Manasquan Inlet, Barnegat Inlet, Absecon Inlet, and Cape May, mark where the Inland Navigation Rules end and the International Rules (COLREGS) begin farther offshore
choice_d: Only state law, never federal law, governs which navigation rules apply on New Jersey waters
explanation: Under 33 CFR Part 80, COLREGS Demarcation Lines are drawn across the entrances to harbors, inlets, and bays along the New Jersey coast, including at Manasquan Inlet, Barnegat Inlet, Absecon Inlet, and Cape May; the Inland Navigation Rules apply on the shoreward side of these lines, while the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) apply seaward of them.
source_note: COLREGS Demarcation Lines, New Jersey coast (33 CFR 80.501-80.503)

question: What does it mean for a large commercial vessel, such as a cargo ship on the Delaware River or Delaware Bay, to be 'constrained by her draft' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: She is any vessel that has run aground and cannot move at all
choice_b: She is a sailing vessel that has lowered its sails and is drifting
choice_c: It refers only to a vessel that has voluntarily anchored in a channel
choice_d: She is a power-driven vessel that, because of her draft in relation to the available depth and width of navigable water, is severely restricted in her ability to deviate from her course
explanation: The Navigation Rules define a vessel constrained by her draft as a power-driven vessel that, because of the relationship between her draft and the available water depth and width, is severely restricted in her ability to deviate from the course she is following, which is why small-boat operators on deep-draft waterways like the Delaware River and Bay should give such vessels a wide berth.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules general definitions (Rule 3(h), 33 CFR 83)
